explanations.answer: The desert road from Jerusalem to Gaza
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The angel says, “Get up and go south to the desert road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza.” (Acts 8:26) That's a road name and a direction, and the next verse says Philip started out. I once followed a recipe with less detail than that, and the cookies still came out better than my first attempts.

explanations.answer: The road down from Jerusalem to Jericho
explanations.explanation: Good guess, friend, because that road shows up in another Bible story. In that one, Jesus tells of a man going down from Jerusalem to Jericho (Luke 10:30). Here the angel names a different road, the desert road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza (Acts 8:26). Two roads out of one city, and only one of them is on Philip's schedule today.

explanations.answer: The highway up from Bethel to Shechem
explanations.explanation: Bethel and Shechem aren't on Philip's map today. The angel sends him south, to the desert road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza (Acts 8:26). Notice it's a road going DOWN from Jerusalem, not up from anywhere. If I got those directions wrong, I'd be standing there with a tray of raw dough wondering why nothing was happening.
Yes, baker. The text says he “…had gone to Jerusalem to worship…” (Acts 8:27) That's a long trip for a man with a big job, and he made it anyway. I think that tells you where his heart was.

I get it, friend. He's a treasury official, so money is the first thing your mind grabs. But the text never mentions a tax. It says he “…had gone to Jerusalem to worship…” (Acts 8:27) He's a treasury man on a worship trip, and the only thing he's in charge of is the entire treasury of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians.

Horses make sense with a chariot in the story, I'll give you that. But the text says nothing about shopping. He “…had gone to Jerusalem to worship…” (Acts 8:27) Horses would have been a very different trip, and a very different story.
Not quite, friend. It's the exact opposite. The Spirit tells Philip, “Go over to that chariot and stay by it.” (Acts 8:29) Stay AWAY would be a very short story. Philip goes right up to that chariot.

That's right, baker. The Spirit says, “Go over to that chariot and stay by it.” (Acts 8:29) Not away, but BY it. Philip got a clear order and ran straight toward it, which is more than I can say for me with a dirty mixing bowl.

explanations.answer: Do you understand what you are reading
explanations.explanation: There it is, baker. Philip asks, “Do you understand what you are reading?” (Acts 8:30) He doesn't open with a speech or a sales pitch. He opens with a question, which I think is a pretty kind way to walk up to a stranger.

explanations.answer: Where did you get that scroll
explanations.explanation: Reasonable question, friend, but Philip doesn't ask it. He asks, “Do you understand what you are reading?” (Acts 8:30) He heard the man reading Isaiah the prophet and went straight to what he was reading.

explanations.answer: Why are you reading it out here
explanations.explanation: Out on a desert road, I can see why you'd wonder. But that isn't what Philip says. He asks, “Do you understand what you are reading?” (Acts 8:30) His question is about the reading itself.

Close, but no, baker. The official says, “How can I… unless someone guides me?” (Acts 8:31) He's honest that he needs a guide. That takes some humility, especially from a man in charge of a whole treasury.

That's right, friend. He answers, “How can I… unless someone guides me?” (Acts 8:31) A powerful official admits he needs a guide and invites Philip to come up and sit with him. That's honest, and I wish I'd had that kind of honesty back when my stamps came out blurry.

explanations.answer: Whether the prophet means himself or someone else
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. He asks, “Tell me… who is the prophet talking about, himself or someone else?” (Acts 8:34) It's a sharp question, and he asks it right out loud. I think a man who asks that is paying close attention.

explanations.answer: Whether the prophet wrote it while in Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: Nice try, friend, but the official never asks where the prophet was standing. He asks, “who is the prophet talking about, himself or someone else?” (Acts 8:34) His question is about WHO the words are about, not where they were written.

explanations.answer: Whether the prophet saw these things in a dream
explanations.explanation: Dreams are in a lot of stories, so I see why that one tempted you. But the official asks something else. He wants to know, “who is the prophet talking about, himself or someone else?” (Acts 8:34) No dreams in his question at all.

That's it, baker. Philip “…began with this very Scripture and told him the good news about Jesus.” (Acts 8:35) He started right where the man was reading, and I love that. No detours, just the page in front of them.

Moses is a big name in Scripture, so I understand the pull. But the text says Philip “…told him the good news about Jesus.” (Acts 8:35) He started with the Isaiah passage the man was reading, and it led him to Jesus.

Elijah is a big name, but he isn't the one here. Philip “…began with this very Scripture and told him the good news about Jesus.” (Acts 8:35) He started with the passage the man was reading, and it led him to Jesus.

Yes, baker. The official says, “Look, here is water! What is there to prevent me from being baptized?” (Acts 8:36) They're traveling along the road when they come to some water, and he speaks right up. I think that man was READY.

Not this time, friend. The official does ask it. As they travel along the road and come to some water, he says, “Look, here is water! What is there to prevent me from being baptized?” (Acts 8:36) He spots the water and speaks right up.
That's right, baker. He “…went on his way rejoicing.” (Acts 8:39) The eunuch saw Philip no more, but he went on his way full of joy. That's a happy ending.
I can see why you'd think that, since Philip just vanished. But the text says the eunuch “…saw him no more, but went on his way rejoicing.” (Acts 8:39) Rejoicing is the word the text gives us.

He was reading Isaiah and asking questions back at the chariot, friend, so I see why searching came to mind. But by the end the text says he “…went on his way rejoicing.” (Acts 8:39) Rejoicing is how he left.

explanations.answer: Preaches the gospel in every town to Caesarea
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Philip “…appeared at Azotus and traveled through that region, preaching the gospel in all the towns until he came to Caesarea.” (Acts 8:40) The Spirit carried him off, and he just kept right on working. I'd have needed a nap and a cookie, maybe four.

explanations.answer: Heads straight back to the apostles in Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: That sounds sensible, friend, but the text goes a different way. Philip “…appeared at Azotus and traveled through that region, preaching the gospel in all the towns until he came to Caesarea.” (Acts 8:40) Nothing about Jerusalem there. He's busy preaching town after town.

explanations.answer: Rests in Azotus until the angel comes back
explanations.explanation: A rest sounds lovely, I won't lie. But the text says Philip “…appeared at Azotus and traveled through that region, preaching the gospel in all the towns until he came to Caesarea.” (Acts 8:40) Nobody is waiting on an angel here. He's on the move and preaching in every town.
